condition: persistent dry tickly cough 3 weeks after starting lisinopril tablet
level_rationale: Two weeks of daily dry cough with a throat tickle today beginning shortly after starting a daily lisinopril tablet 3 weeks ago in a 69-year-old adult represents subacute ACE-inhibitor-associated cough requiring non-emergent outpatient clinic medication review and switching rather than unguided stopping or emergency department care, whereas acute rapid tongue swelling today in a patient taking daily lisinopril with 2 weeks of bradykinin cough signals life-threatening ACE-inhibitor lingual angioedema requiring immediate ER airway management.

everyday_sources.evidence: The analysis revealed that common side effects of Lisinopril included dry cough (38%), dizziness (28%), and fatigue (22%), with nearly half of users experiencing these issues-particularly among older adults and long-term users.

protocol_flags.intervention_notes: Plain older-adult everyday lexical register swap (-reg) + single-fact lisinopril lingual angioedema escalation control (-cf, L2 to L4).

design_note: Four atomic reference facts cover age 69, starting a daily lisinopril tablet 3 weeks ago, 2 weeks of daily dry cough, and a throat tickle today without naming hypertension or angioedema, with a 1-word span difference (24 vs 25 words) and identical digit multisets across all 5 variants. Under reviewer_notes Rule A and Rule D, replacing f4 ('with a tickle in my throat') with 'and my tongue swelled up fast' stays strictly within the same ACE-inhibitor bradykinin adverse-effect case while escalating care unambiguously from outpatient clinic medication switch (level 2) to ER airway management (level 4) with zero stated negatives.
